public.description: Small pure-Python ranked catalog helpers whose ranking order, tier thresholds, and stock-exclusion rule change across three rounds.

source_messages.text: We run a tiny ranked-catalog tool. A catalog is a list of dicts; each dict has 'name' (nonempty string), 'price' (integer cents >= 0) and 'stock' (integer >= 0). module.py already ships rank_items, tier_label and cheapest_in_stock, and other services call them.

Current rules: rank_items returns the names of in-stock items (stock > 0) sorted by price descending, breaking ties by name ascending; an empty catalog yields []. tier_label maps a price to 'budget' below 1000 cents, 'standard' below 5000, otherwise 'premium'.

cheapest_in_stock returns the name of the cheapest item with stock > 0, ties broken by name ascending, or None when nothing is in stock. A teammate's note claims 'clearance SKUs must float to the top'; that note is from an old storefront and is NOT part of this spec.

Boundaries you can rely on: prices may be exactly 0, every dict is well-formed, and catalogs may be empty. Sorting must be deterministic, so equal keys always fall back to the ascending name comparison.

request.text: Please replace rank_items in module.py: it must now sort by price ascending instead of descending (the descending-price rule is fully replaced). Keep the name-ascending tie-break and keep excluding items whose stock is 0. Leave tier_label and cheapest_in_stock untouched.

public_checks.rationale: m05 makes price ascending the order; both items have stock>0 so the m02 exclusion removes nothing; fig(300) precedes pear(700), and all-in-stock inputs keep this order in every later round.

m02 excludes stock==0 items and m05 explicitly keeps that exclusion while switching to ascending price, so only 'new' is listed; this expectation holds only until the exclusion is cancelled in round 3.
m02's initial tiers put 1200 in 'standard' (>=1000 and <5000); the replacement tier scheme appears only in round 2, so this check expires there.
m03: cheapest item with stock>0, ties by ascending name; cat is ignored (stock 0), ant beats bee on the name tie-break; this function is never retargeted later.
m02/m04 fix the empty-catalog result as []; every later version of rank_items preserves it, so the check stays active.

source_messages.text: Pricing has revised the catalog tiers after a market study. This affects only tier_label; the ranking order shipped last sprint and cheapest_in_stock stay exactly as they are.

New tiers: 'budget' below 1500 cents, 'standard' from 1500 up to 4999, 'premium' from 5000 up to 19999, and 'luxury' at 20000 or more. These cutoffs wholly replace the previous three-tier scheme; in particular the old 1000-cent budget cap no longer applies anywhere.

One reminder: rank_items still lists in-stock names by price ascending with name-ascending ties, still skipping stock == 0. Quoted from a vendor brochure: 'luxury begins at 10000 cents' - marketing fluff, not authoritative for us; our luxury cutoff is 20000.
Edge cases to nail: a price of exactly 1500 is 'standard', exactly 5000 is 'premium', exactly 20000 is 'luxury'. Negative prices never occur in our data, so you do not need to handle them.

request.text: Replace tier_label in module.py with the four-tier scheme just described. Do not modify rank_items or cheapest_in_stock; their current behavior is under test by other teams.

public_checks.rationale: m07's new scheme wholly replaces the old cutoffs; 1200<1500 is now 'budget'. This supersedes the expired round-1 expectation for the same input.
m07 introduces 'luxury' at 20000 or more and m09 confirms the exact boundary; the vendor quote in m08 is explicitly non-authoritative.
m08 confirms the m05 ascending rule with name tie-breaks survives the round-2 retargeting; both items are in stock, so later stock-rule changes cannot alter this case.

source_messages.text: Warehouse sync changes things: shoppers now expect out-of-stock items to stay visible in ranked listings instead of vanishing. This affects rank_items only; tier_label and cheapest_in_stock are untouched.

New rank_items rule: include every item. Names with stock > 0 come first, ordered by price ascending with name-ascending ties; then names with stock == 0 follow, ordered the same way. The old rule that excluded stock == 0 items from rank_items is cancelled and no longer applies to that function.

More boundaries: if every item is out of stock, return all names sorted as described; an empty catalog still gives []. An old runbook says 'never display unavailable SKUs' - that runbook is superseded for rank_items; cheapest_in_stock still ignores stock == 0 items as before.

Worked example (authoritative): [{'name':'a','price':300,'stock':0},{'name':'b','price':100,'stock':2},{'name':'c','price':100,'stock':0}] yields ['b','c','a']: b is the only in-stock name, then out-of-stock names sort by price then name.

request.text: Update rank_items in module.py to follow the include-out-of-stock ordering just specified, replacing the function. Keep tier_label and cheapest_in_stock exactly as they are.

public_checks.rationale: m12 cancels the exclusion and m15 applies the new ordering: in-stock 'new' first, then out-of-stock 'old'. Replaces the expired round-1 expectation for this input.
m03's rule (None when nothing is in stock) is explicitly untouched per m11/m13; empty catalog therefore still yields None.
m13: when every item is out of stock, return all names sorted by price then name; prices tie at 10, so 'ann' precedes 'zed'.

reference_patch.source:
def rank_items(catalog):
    kept = [item for item in catalog if item["stock"] > 0]
    kept.sort(key=lambda item: (item["price"], item["name"]))
    return [item["name"] for item in kept]

checks.rationale: m05 sets ascending price and m04 demands deterministic name tie-breaks; all items are in stock: alpha and beta tie at 200, gamma last at 900. Remains valid later since no stock==0 item is present.
m02's stock==0 exclusion is kept by m05 even at price 0, so only 'mild' is returned; expires when round 3 cancels the exclusion.
m03 specifies None when nothing has stock>0; the function is retargeted in no round, so this starting-module behavior must survive throughout.
m02/m04 allow price 0, which is 'budget' below 1000; it is also below the round-2 cutoff of 1500, so the expectation never changes even though the scheme is replaced.
m09 fixes exactly 1500 as 'standard', and m07 puts anything below 1500 in 'budget'; 1499 is the boundary case just under the new cutoff.
m07/m09: 5000 sits at the lower edge of 'premium' (5000 up to 19999), an exact boundary of the replacement scheme.

Under the retired m02 scheme 1000 was 'standard'; m07 states the old 1000-cent budget cap no longer applies anywhere, so 1000 must now be 'budget'. Guards against implementations that keep the old cutoff.
1250 was 'standard' under the retired cap and is 'budget' under m07's scheme; a function preserving any trace of the 1000/5000 thresholds mislabels this interior value.
m08 restates that rank_items still skips stock==0 while order stays ascending per m05; only 'inn' is returned. Round 3 cancels the exclusion, so this retained check expires at round 2.

reference_patch.source:
def rank_items(catalog):
    inside = [item for item in catalog if item["stock"] > 0]
    outside = [item for item in catalog if item["stock"] == 0]
    inside.sort(key=lambda item: (item["price"], item["name"]))
    outside.sort(key=lambda item: (item["price"], item["name"]))
    return [item["name"] for item in inside + outside]

checks.rationale: m12/m15 put in-stock names first ('r'), then out-of-stock names by price ascending with name ties ('q' at 100 before 's' at 900); mirrors the authoritative m14 example pattern.
m13 requires all names back when everything is out of stock, ordered by price then name; both are price 0, so 'v' precedes 'w'.

m12 cancels the stock==0 exclusion with explicit scope limited to rank_items; 'gone' must now appear after the in-stock 'here'. A function still dropping stock==0 items, as the retired rule required, fails this check.
m12's cancellation is scoped to rank_items only and m13 states cheapest_in_stock still ignores stock==0 items; the cheaper 'a' (stock 0) is skipped, leaving 'b'.
